docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Module 4

Scheduled Black Wed, Aug 12, 2026 and Fri, Aug 14, 2026 · Gold Thu, Aug 13, 2026 and Mon, Aug 17, 2026

7253 Software Development Capstone · self-guided · work at your own pace

🎯 Objective

By the end of this module you can:

  • Pull values out of objects and arrays with destructuring, including in a function's parameter list
  • Copy and extend objects and arrays with spread, without touching the original
  • Gather leftovers with rest — and say how it differs from spread
  • Build strings with template literals instead of +
  • Give a parameter a default value and say exactly when it fires
🔑 Why it matters

No module in Part 1 is closer to React than this one. The others teach you ideas React is built on. This one teaches you the literal characters React code is written in.

In this module In React Object destructuring in a parameter function Card({ title, price }) — how every component reads its props Array destructuring const [count, setCount] = useState(0) — how every hook is read Spread in an object setUser({ ...user, name: "new" }) — the way state updates are written Rest in a parameter function Button({ label, ...rest }) — passing extra props through Template literals className={`btn ${active ? "on" : ""}`} — every dynamic string Default parameters function Card({ size = "md" }) — default props

Read that table again after you finish the build. Every row will have stopped being syntax and started being something you have typed.

Nothing here is a new idea. Every one of these is shorthand for something you already do the long way. That is exactly why it is worth taking seriously: shorthand you half-know is worse than shorthand you don't know at all, because you will read it in every tutorial you ever open and quietly guess at it.

📖 Learn Topic Go-to resource Destructuring — the whole thing javascript.info: Destructuring assignment Template literals javascript.info: Strings Spread and rest javascript.info: Rest parameters and spread syntax Default parameters javascript.info: Function basics — default values

The destructuring page is the one to read properly. Do the object-destructuring section before the array one — object destructuring is the one you will use every day in React, and the array section makes more sense once the object version has landed.

The one idea underneath all of it

Taking things apart, and putting them back together.

  • Destructuring takes something apart: give me the pieces I want, by name.
  • Spread puts it back together: pour everything out into a new one.
  • Rest gathers what's left: and collect the leftovers under this name.
const game = { title: "Celeste", year: 2018, price: 20 };

const { title, year } = game;              // apart
const cheaper = { ...game, price: 15 };    // back together, brand new object
console.log(game.price);                   // 20 — the original never moved

That last line is the same "unchanged" you proved in Module 3, and it is the same one Module 5 is entirely about. Three modules in a row circling the same point is not an accident.

Spread and rest are the same three dots doing opposite jobs

This trips everybody. The dots mean unpack or gather depending on which side of the = they are on.

You wrote The dots are doing You get const copy = { ...game } Spreading — pouring game out into a new object A new object with all of game's properties const { title, ...rest } = game Resting — gathering what you didn't name rest holds everything except title sum(...numbers) Spreading — the array becomes separate arguments sum(1, 2, 3) function sum(...nums) Resting — the arguments become one array nums is [1, 2, 3]

On the right of the =, or in a call: spreading. On the left, or in a parameter list: gathering.

⌨️ Build — syntax.js

In your capstone folder, make syntax.js. Run it as you go with node syntax.js.

Reuse Module 3's dataset. Copy the games array from data.js to the top of this file — same six games. You are about to write Module 3's code again, shorter.

1 · Template literals
  1. Rewrite Module 3's "Celeste (2018)" map using backticks instead of +
  2. Build one multi-line string — a little receipt for one game, three lines, one pair of backticks
  3. Put an actual expression inside a ${} — not just a variable. ${game.price * 0.9} or a ternary

✅ No + anywhere in your string building, and one ${} contains real work.

2 · Object destructuring
  1. const { title, year } = games[0] — the basic form
  2. Rename on the way out: pull title into a variable called name
  3. Give a default: pull publisher — which no game has — and default it to "unknown"
  4. The important one: rewrite a Module 3 callback so the parameter is destructured. g => g.title becomes ({ title }) => title

✅ Part 4 works, and you can say what the braces in the parameter list are doing.

Part 4 is function Card({ title, price }). That is not an analogy — it is the same syntax doing the same job. Every React component you write in Part 2 starts this way.

3 · Array destructuring
  1. const [first, second] = games — grab the first two
  2. Skip one: get the third game without naming the first two
  3. Swap two variables in a single line, no temp variable

✅ You can say why arrays destructure by position and objects destructure by name.

4 · Spread — and the update that matters
  1. Copy the games array into a new array, then push onto the copy. Prove games is unchanged
  2. Copy one game object, then merge: { ...game, price: 15 }
  3. Merge two objects and find out which one wins when both have the same key

✅ The original games still has six items and the original game still has its old price.

This is the React state update, exactly: setUser({ ...user, name: "new" }). Every single state update in Part 2 is this line with different words.

Now the one that costs people a week in October — spread is shallow:

const original = { title: "Hades", tags: ["roguelike", "indie"] };
const copy = { ...original };
copy.tags.push("greek");
console.log(original.tags);   // ["roguelike", "indie", "greek"]  ← !

Run it. copy is a new object, but copy.tags and original.tags are the same array. Write in your notes what you think is going on. You do not have to solve it — Module 5 is this problem — but you do have to have seen it.

5 · Rest
  1. const { title, ...details } = games[0] — what ends up in details?
  2. Write tally(...nums) that takes any number of arguments and adds them up
  3. Call it with a spread array: tally(...[1, 2, 3])

✅ You used ... to gather in one place and to unpack in another, and you can say which was which.

6 · Default parameters

Write describe(game, currency = "$") that returns a template-literal string.

Then call it three ways and record what you get:

describe(games[0]);              // default fires
describe(games[0], "£");         // default does not fire
describe(games[0], undefined);   // ← predict this one before you run it
describe(games[0], null);        // ← and this one

✅ You can say exactly which of the four calls used the default, and why null behaves differently from undefined.

Stretch · Rewrite Module 3

Take your chained expression from Module 3 part 5 — "the total hours I've spent on games I haven't finished" — and rewrite it using destructured callback parameters and a template literal for the output.

Put the old version and the new version next to each other in your notes. Same logic, same answer, noticeably less noise. That difference is the entire argument for this module.

🔭 Looking ahead — pick two APIs

Five minutes, and it pays off for the rest of the semester.

Your Part 1 project is a Data App built on a free public API. Open the API table in the Projects — semester 1 doc and shortlist two that actually interest you.

You are not committing to anything yet — you lock one in when the build block opens on Sep 9/10. But from here on, when a module teaches you something, you will have a real dataset in mind to imagine it against, and that makes all of it stick better.

Check both work on the school network before you get attached to one.

✅ Check yourself

Can you, without looking anything up:

  • ☐ Destructure an object inside a function's parameter list?
  • ☐ Say why { ...game, price: 15 } doesn't change game?
  • ☐ Explain the difference between the ... in { ...game } and the ... in { title, ...rest }?
  • ☐ Put an expression, not just a variable, inside a ${}?
  • ☐ Say when a default parameter fires and when it doesn't?

If any box is unchecked, spend twenty minutes on that row's resource. Then check it.

🏁 Done when
  • syntax.js runs and covers all six parts
  • At least one function parameter is destructured — not just a variable
  • Your immutable update produces a new object and you printed the original to prove it is untouched
  • The shallow-copy surprise is in your notes, in your own words
  • Your log entry is written — what you built, what confused you and how you got past it, any AI use, and the URL of anything you looked up
  • build check: run it, show me the immutable update, and tell me what the three dots are doing in two different lines of your file. Five minutes.

Next: Module 5 — Objects & Immutability — where the shallow-copy surprise from part 4 stops being a surprise and becomes the whole subject.

docs.title: Objects & ImmutabilityPart 1 · Module 5 — Objects & Immutability
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Module 5

Scheduled Black Tue, Aug 18, 2026 · Gold Wed, Aug 19, 2026

7253 Software Development Capstone · self-guided · work at your own pace

🎯 Objective

By the end of this module you can:

  • Explain the difference between two names for one object and two separate objects
  • Say what question React actually asks when it decides whether to re-render
  • Update an object without changing the original, at any depth
  • Add to, remove from, and update one item in an array of objects — immutably
  • Spot the shallow-copy trap before it costs you an afternoon
🔑 Why it matters

This is the module that decides whether React works for you or fights you.

Every "why isn't my component updating?" question in Part 2 has the same answer, and it is in this module.

In this moduleIn React before !== afterExactly what React checks to decide whether to re-render { ...state, open: true }setState — every single time items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, done: true } : i)Toggling one item in a list items.filter(i => i.id !== id)Deleting an item The shallow-copy trapThe single most common React state bug

React never looks inside your object. It asks one question: is this the same object I had last time? If you changed the object in place, the answer is yes, and nothing happens on screen. Your data is right and your app looks broken.

📖 Learn TopicGo-to resource Objects and referencesjavascript.info: Object references and copying Object basicsjavascript.info: Objects Spread on objectsjavascript.info: Rest and spread Why React needs thisreact.dev: Updating objects in state

Read the react.dev page even though you have not written any React yet. It is short, and it is the clearest explanation of why any of this matters. You will understand it — it is all JavaScript.

The one idea underneath all of it

**A variable holding an object holds a reference — an address, not the thing.**

const alias = player;
alias.level = 99;
console.log(player.level);   // 99

Nothing was copied. Both names point at the same object, so changing one changes "both," because there was only ever one.

Everything in this module follows from that sentence. Read it twice.

⌨️ Build — state.js

In your capstone folder, make state.js. Run it as you go with node state.js.

Start with this:

const player = {
  name: "Sam",
  level: 7,
  settings: { theme: "dark", sound: true },
  inventory: [
    { id: 1, item: "sword",  qty: 1 },
    { id: 2, item: "potion", qty: 3 },
    { id: 3, item: "rope",   qty: 2 },
  ],
};
1 · Two names, one object
  1. Make alias = player, change alias.level, and print player.level
  2. Print alias === player
  3. Set the level back to 7
  4. Now make copy = { ...player } and print copy === player

Done when: You can say why step 1 changed something you never named.

2 · The question React actually asks

Write this function and use it:

function reactWouldRerender(before, after) {
  return before !== after;
}

Call it twice — once with the same object passed as both arguments, once with an object you replaced. Print both results.

Done when: You can explain, in one sentence, why mutating state is invisible to React.

3 · Change one field, keep the rest 
const levelledUp = { ...player, level: player.level + 1 };

Print the new level, the original level, and levelledUp !== player.

Done when: All three are what you expected.

4 · The shallow-copy trap

This is the part to slow down for.

  1. Make shallow = { ...player }
  2. Print shallow.settings === player.settings

It is true. A spread copies one level only — the nested settings object is still shared, so changing shallow.settings.theme would change the original's too.

  1. Now do it correctly, spreading every level you are changing:
const themed = {
  ...player,
  settings: { ...player.settings, theme: "light" },
};
  1. Prove the original theme is untouched, and that themed.settings is a new object
  2. Print themed.inventory === player.inventory — it is true, and that is fine

Done when: You can say why step 5 being true is correct rather than a bug.

You only copy what you change. Sharing the parts you did not touch is not laziness — it is what makes React fast. It can skip anything whose reference is unchanged.

5 · The three array updates

These three patterns cover essentially every list operation you will write in React.

ADD — spread, never push:

const added = { ...player, inventory: [...player.inventory, { id: 4, item: "torch", qty: 5 }] };

REMOVE — filter, never splice:

const removed = { ...player, inventory: player.inventory.filter(i => i.id !== 1) };

UPDATE ONE — map, and spread the one that matches:

const used = {
  ...player,
  inventory: player.inventory.map(i => i.id === 2 ? { ...i, qty: i.qty - 1 } : i),
};

Then print these two:

used.inventory[0] === player.inventory[0]   // true  — untouched item reused
used.inventory[1] !== player.inventory[1]   // true  — changed item replaced

Done when: You can explain why one is true and the other is false, and why that is exactly what you want.

6 · Prove nothing moved

At the very end, print player and confirm it is identical to what you started with. Every operation above produced something new and left the original alone.

Done when: Level 7, dark theme, three items, three potions.

Stretch · Object.freeze and structuredClone 
const frozen = Object.freeze({ ...player });
frozen.level = 1000;
console.log(frozen.level);      // still 7 — the write was ignored

Then find out that freeze is shallow too — frozen.settings.sound is still writable. Same trap, different tool.

Then try structuredClone(player), which goes all the way down and shares nothing.

Why not just use structuredClone everywhere? Work out the answer. It has to do with the thing that makes React fast.

✅ Check Yourself

Can you, without looking anything up:

  • Explain what a variable holding an object actually holds?
  • Say what question React asks to decide whether to re-render?
  • Write an immutable update to one field?
  • Write an immutable update to a nested field?
  • Add, remove, and update one item in an array of objects?
  • Explain why the untouched items are deliberately the same objects?

If any box is unchecked, spend twenty minutes on that row's resource. Then check it.

🏁 Done When
  • state.js runs and covers all six parts
  • player is unchanged at the end — print it and prove it
  • Your log entry is written — what you built, what confused you and how you resolved it, any AI use, and the URL of anything you looked up
  • build check: run it, then I will describe a change to a nested value and ask you to write the update live. Five minutes.

Next: Module 6 — Classes & OOP — encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. Not because React uses classes (it does not), but because the ideas are everywhere else in the field.

docs.title: Classes & OOPPart 1 · Module 6 — Classes & OOP
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Module 6

Scheduled Black Thu, Aug 20, 2026 · Gold Fri, Aug 21, 2026

7253 Software Development Capstone · self-guided · work at your own pace

🎯 Objective

By the end of this module you can:

  • Write a class with a constructor, methods, getters and setters
  • Keep data private and validate it on the way in
  • Extend a class and call super
  • Override a method, and explain what polymorphism buys you
  • Say why React moved away from classes
🔑 Why it matters

Be told this up front: React function components do not use classes. You will not write a class in Part 2.

This module is here for the ideas, which are standards D1.2 and D1.5 and which are everywhere else in software:

IdeaWhere you meet it again EncapsulationEvery API you consume — you call methods, you don't touch internals InheritanceJava (your other course), C#, Python, Swift — nearly everything but React PolymorphismOne loop handling many types — the idea behind most plugin systems Getters and settersValidation at the boundary; you will meet this in databases too

There is also a genuinely interesting reason React left classes behind, and the stretch section is about that. Understanding what was wrong with classes is a better reason to like hooks than being told hooks are modern.

📖 Learn TopicGo-to resource Class basicsjavascript.info: Class basic syntax Inheritancejavascript.info: Class inheritance Getters, setters, privatejavascript.info: Property flags and private fields Staticjavascript.info: Static properties and methods

If you are taking Software Development as well, this module will feel familiar. Java does all of this. The syntax differs; the ideas do not. Say so at the build check — connecting the two courses is worth marks in both.

The one idea underneath all of it

A class is a template. An object is one thing made from it.

Everything else — inheritance, polymorphism, private fields — is a refinement of "how do I avoid writing the same template twice."

⌨️ Build — classes.js

In your capstone folder, make classes.js. Run it as you go with node classes.js.

1 · A class 
class Item {
  constructor(name, price) {
    this.name = name;
    this.price = price;
  }

  describe() {
    return `${this.name} — $${this.price}`;
  }
}
  1. Make one with new Item("rope", 8) and call describe()
  2. Add a toString() method that returns describe(), then put the object directly inside a template literal and watch it work
  3. Print rope instanceof Item

Done when: Item 2 surprises people. ${obj} calls toString() automatically.

2 · Getters, setters, and a private field 
class Account {
  #balance = 0;

  constructor(owner, opening = 0) {
    this.owner = owner;
    this.#balance = opening;
  }

  get balance() { return this.#balance; }

  set balance(value) {
    if (value < 0) throw new RangeError("balance cannot be negative");
    this.#balance = value;
  }

  deposit(amount) {
    this.balance = this.#balance + amount;
    return this;
  }
}
  1. Make an account and print acct.balance — no parentheses. It looks like a property and runs like a method
  2. Chain two deposits: acct.deposit(5).deposit(10). Work out why that works
  3. Try to set a negative balance inside a try/catch and print the error message
  4. Try to reach #balance from outside the class

Done when: You can explain what return this is doing in deposit, and why #balance is different from just naming something _balance.

3 · Static 
class Money {
  static rate = 0.07;
  static tax(amount) { return +(amount * Money.rate).toFixed(2); }
}

Call Money.tax(40) without making a Money. Then confirm an instance does not have tax on it.

Done when: You can say what "belongs to the class, not the instance" means.

4 · Inheritance

Write Weapon extends Item with an extra damage, and Potion extends Item with an extra heals. Both override describe() and both call super.describe() inside it.

constructor(name, price, damage) {
  super(name, price);     // must come first
  this.damage = damage;
}
  1. Make a Weapon and print its description
  2. Print sword instanceof Weapon and sword instanceof Item

Done when: Both are true, and you can say why.

super() must come before any use of this. Move it to the second line and Java— sorry, JavaScript — refuses to run it. Try it once so you recognise the error.

5 · Polymorphism — the payoff

Put an Item, a Weapon and a Potion in one array and loop over them:

for (const thing of bag) {
  console.log(thing.describe());
}

The loop never checks what anything is. Each object knows its own describe().

Then do the real test: write a brand-new Armour extends Item, push one into the bag, and run the same loop again without changing it.

Done when: That is polymorphism, and the fact that you changed nothing is the whole point.

Stretch · Why React left classes behind

Write the same "counter" idea two ways.

As a closure — no this, no new:

function makeCounter(start = 0) {
  let count = start;
  return {
    increment: () => ++count,
    get value() { return count; },
  };
}

Then find the this problem:

class Broken {
  constructor() { this.label = "works"; }
  show() { return this.label; }
}
const b = new Broken();
const loose = b.show;    // pulled off the object
loose();                 // throws

Wrap that call in try/catch and print the error type. Then make it work with b.show.bind(b)().

That is why old React components were full of .bind(this). Hooks exist partly to make the whole problem go away.

✅ Check Yourself

Can you, without looking anything up:

  • Write a class with a constructor and a method?
  • Explain the difference between a getter and a method?
  • Say what # does that a naming convention cannot?
  • Explain why super() has to come first?
  • Say what polymorphism let you avoid writing?
  • Describe the this problem in one sentence?

If any box is unchecked, spend twenty minutes on that row's resource. Then check it.

🏁 Done When
  • classes.js runs and covers all five parts
  • Adding Armour required no change to the loop
  • Your log entry is written — what you built, what confused you and how you resolved it, any AI use, and the URL of anything you looked up
  • build check: run it, then tell me one thing classes do well and one thing that made React abandon them. Five minutes.

Next: Module 7 — Data Structures — Map, Set, and choosing the right shape for the job, which matters more than any syntax in this module.

docs.title: Data StructuresPart 1 · Module 7 — Data Structures
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Module 7

Scheduled Black Mon, Aug 24, 2026 and Wed, Aug 26, 2026 · Gold Tue, Aug 25, 2026 and Thu, Aug 27, 2026

7253 Software Development Capstone · self-guided · work at your own pace

🎯 Objective

By the end of this module you can:

  • Build a stack and say what LIFO means
  • Build a queue and say why shift() is the wrong tool at scale
  • Build a linked list and explain what a node is
  • Choose between an array, a Map, and a Set for a given job
  • Say what Big-O notation is actually trying to tell you
🔑 Why it matters

You will not hand-write a linked list in React. You will choose between an array and a Map almost every day.

Both halves of this module are here on purpose. The classic structures are standards D1.8–D1.10 and they are how you learn what "fast" means. Map and Set are the ones you will reach for on Thursday.

IdeaWhere you meet it again StackUndo. Browser back. The call stack your errors are printed from. QueueJob queues, print spoolers, React's own render queue — anything first-come-first-served Linked listReact's fiber tree is one. So is every structure where you insert in the middle a lot. Map / SetEvery day. Lookup by key, and "have I already seen this one?"

The stretch section is where this module earns its place. You will make a queue slow, measure it, then make it fast — and Big-O will stop being a definition you memorised.

📖 Learn TopicGo-to resource Map and Setjavascript.info: Map and Set Arrays as stacks and queuesjavascript.info: Arrays Recursion and the call stackjavascript.info: Recursion and stack Reference for bothMDN: Map · MDN: Set

If you are taking Software Development as well, you will build these again in Java. Same structures, different syntax, and the Java version makes you say the types out loud. Naming the connection at the build check is worth marks in both courses.

The one idea underneath all of it

A data structure is a promise about what is fast.

Picking one is picking which operation you want to be cheap — and accepting that something else will be expensive. There is no structure that is best at everything, which is exactly why there is more than one.

⌨️ Build — structures.js

In your capstone folder, make structures.js. Run it as you go with node structures.js.

1 · A stack — last in, first out 
const stack = [];
stack.push("a");
stack.push("b");
console.log(stack.pop());   // "b" — the last one in
  1. Push three things, pop two, print what is left
  2. Now wrap it: write a Stack class with push, pop, peek, and a size getter
  3. Make pop on an empty stack return undefined rather than crashing — decide that deliberately

Done when: You can say what LIFO means without expanding the letters, and your Stack hides the array completely. Nobody outside the class should be able to reach in and splice it.

You have been using a stack all along. Print a stack trace from a thrown error and read it bottom to top — that is the call stack, and it is this exact structure.

2 · A queue — first in, first out 
const queue = [];
queue.push("a");
queue.push("b");
console.log(queue.shift());   // "a" — the first one in
  1. Write a Queue class with enqueue, dequeue, peek, size
  2. Enqueue five, dequeue two, print what remains
  3. Read the docs for shift() and find the sentence about it being slower than pop()

Done when: Your queue works, and you can say why shift() is not free: it re-indexes every remaining element. On five items that is nothing. Part 5 is where it stops being nothing.

3 · A linked list — the one you build by hand 
class Node {
  constructor(value) {
    this.value = value;
    this.next = null;      // the whole idea, right here
  }
}

A linked list is a chain of nodes. Each one knows its value and the next node. There is no array underneath — that is the point.

  1. Write a LinkedList with head, a push(value) that walks to the end and links on, and a toArray()
  2. Push four values and print toArray()
  3. Add prepend(value) — put a node at the front. Notice how little work it is
  4. Now write unshift's equivalent on an array of 100,000 items and think about what the computer had to do

Done when: prepend is three lines and touches two nodes, no matter how long the list is. Adding to the front of an array moves every single element. That difference is the reason linked lists exist.

Do not skip toArray(). It is how you prove the chain is actually linked, and it is your debugging tool for the rest of the module.

4 · Map and Set — the two you will actually use 
const seen = new Set([1, 2, 2, 3]);
console.log(seen.size);          // 3 — duplicates are gone

const prices = new Map();
prices.set("rope", 8);
console.log(prices.get("rope")); // 8
  1. Take an array with duplicates and dedupe it in one line with a Set
  2. Build a Map of name → price, then loop it with for (const [k, v] of prices)
  3. Try using an object as a Map key. Then try the same thing with a plain {} and watch it fail
  4. Print prices.size, then work out how you would get the same number from a plain object

Done when: You can state two things a Map does that an object cannot: any key type, and a real size. Item 3 is the one that surprises people.

5 · Choosing the shape You need to...Reach for Look something up by name, constantlyMap Know whether you have seen a value beforeSet Keep things in order and read them by positionArray Always take the most recent thingStack Always take the oldest thingQueue Insert in the middle over and overLinked list

Now use it. You have a list of 500 orders and you need to answer "what is order #4471?" a thousand times.

  1. Do it with array.find() — write the line
  2. Do it with a Map keyed by order number — write those lines
  3. Say, in one sentence, what the Map version stopped doing a thousand times

Done when: Your answer to item 3 mentions searching. find() walks the list every single time; the Map goes straight there.

Stretch · Make it slow, then measure it

This is the part that turns Big-O from a definition into something you have seen with your own eyes.

const N = 100_000;
const arr = Array.from({ length: N }, (_, i) => i);

console.time("shift");
while (arr.length) arr.shift();      // re-indexes every time
console.timeEnd("shift");

Then build a queue that never shifts — keep a head index and move it forward instead of removing from the front:

class FastQueue {
  #items = [];
  #head = 0;
  enqueue(v) { this.#items.push(v); }
  dequeue() {
    if (this.#head >= this.#items.length) return undefined;
    return this.#items[this.#head++];    // move the pointer, move nothing else
  }
}
  1. Time 100,000 dequeues from FastQueue the same way
  2. Put the two numbers side by side
  3. Try it again at 10,000 and at 1,000,000, and watch how the gap changes

Done when: The two times are not close, and the gap grows as N grows. That is the entire content of "O(n²) versus O(n)" — you just measured it instead of being told it.

Do not memorise Big-O tables. The useful skill is noticing that a loop contains a hidden loop. shift() inside a while is a loop inside a loop, which is why it fell over.

✅ Check Yourself

Can you, without looking anything up:

  • Say what LIFO and FIFO mean, and give one real example of each?
  • Explain why shift() costs more than pop()?
  • Draw a three-node linked list on paper and label what each node holds?
  • Say one thing a Map can do that a plain object cannot?
  • Say when an array is the wrong choice?
  • Explain what your two timing numbers in the stretch were telling you?

If any box is unchecked, spend twenty minutes on that row's resource. Then check it.

🏁 Done When
  • structures.js runs and covers all five parts
  • Your Stack, Queue, and LinkedList are classes — not loose arrays with comments
  • You have the two timing numbers from the stretch, written down
  • Your log entry is written — what you built, what confused you and how you resolved it, any AI use, and the URL of anything you looked up
  • build check: run it, then talk me through the timing numbers and what they mean. Five minutes.

Next: Module 8 — ES Modules — import and export, and the end of one enormous file. Everything you have written so far has been one script; from here your code lives in pieces that find each other.

docs.title: ES ModulesPart 1 · Module 8 — ES Modules
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Module 8

Scheduled Black Fri, Aug 28, 2026 · Gold Mon, Aug 31, 2026

7253 Software Development Capstone · self-guided · work at your own pace

🎯 Objective

By the end of this module you can:

  • Split one file into several and have them find each other
  • Use named exports and know when to use a default
  • Say what "type": "module" in package.json does
  • Import only what you need, and see why that matters later
  • Recognise a circular import and get yourself out of one
🔑 Why it matters

Every file you have written so far has been one long script. That has been fine. It stops being fine at about two hundred lines.

From here your code lives in pieces. This is the module that makes every React tutorial readable, because the first line of every React file you will ever see is an import.

IdeaWhere you meet it again import / exportThe first line of literally every React component file Named vs defaultimport React from vs import { useState } from — you have already seen both One job per fileHow every codebase bigger than a homework assignment is organised Import only what you needBundle size — the thing that decides whether your deployed app loads fast

This module is short and it is load-bearing. Nothing here is difficult. Getting it wrong makes every later module confusing, because the error messages point at import lines rather than at what is actually broken.

📖 Learn TopicGo-to resource Modules, start to finishjavascript.info: Modules, introduction Export and importjavascript.info: Export and Import ReferenceMDN: JavaScript modules Node specificsNode docs: ECMAScript modules

Java calls this package and import; Python calls it import too. Same problem, three solutions. If you are in 7184 you have already met the idea — what is different here is that the file path is part of the import, which trips people coming from Java.

The one idea underneath all of it

A module is a file that decides what the outside world can see.

Everything you do not export is private to that file — permanently and automatically. You do not have to do anything to get that; it is the default. What takes effort is deciding what to let out.

⌨️ Build — shop/

This time you are building a folder, not a file. In your capstone folder make shop/, and inside it the files below. Run it with node shop/main.js.

1 · Turn modules on

Node needs telling. In your capstone folder, make package.json:

{
  "name": "capstone",
  "type": "module"
}
  1. Create the file exactly as above
  2. Make shop/format.js with one line: export const money = (n) => `$${n.toFixed(2)}`;
  3. Make shop/main.js that imports it and prints money(8)
  4. Run node shop/main.js
// shop/main.js
import { money } from "./format.js";
console.log(money(8));            // $8.00

Done when: It prints $8.00. If you get "Cannot use import statement outside a module", your package.json is missing, in the wrong folder, or missing the "type" line.

The .js on the end of the import is required. Node will not guess it for you. React projects let you drop it because a bundler is doing the guessing — but here, in plain Node, leave it off and it fails.

2 · Named exports — the ones you will use most

Make shop/inventory.js:

export const items = [
  { id: 1, name: "rope",  price: 8 },
  { id: 2, name: "torch", price: 3 },
];

export function find(id) {
  return items.find((i) => i.id === id);
}

export function total() {
  return items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
}
  1. Import only find into main.js and print find(2)
  2. Now import total as well, in the same { }
  3. Rename one on the way in: import { total as cartTotal } from "./inventory.js";
  4. Try to use something you did not import and read the error

Done when: You can import one thing, several things, or a renamed thing, and the error for the fourth item says not defined — which tells you imports are not automatic.

The curly braces are not optional decoration. { find } means "the export named find". Without braces you are asking for the default export, which this file does not have.

3 · A default export, and when to bother

Make shop/Shop.js with one main thing in it:

export default class Shop {
  constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
  open() { return `${this.name} is open`; }
}
  1. Import it with no braces and any name you like: import Store from "./Shop.js";
  2. Prove the name is yours to choose — import it again in a scratch file as Whatever
  3. Add a named export to the same file and import both at once
import Shop, { helper } from "./Shop.js";   // default first, then named

Done when: You can state the rule in one sentence: one default per file, as many named as you like — and you noticed that a default export's name is decided by whoever imports it, which is either convenient or confusing depending on the day.

Prefer named exports. A default whose name changes between files makes code hard to search. Use a default when the file genuinely is one thing — a single React component, for example, which is exactly why React files use them.

4 · One job per file

Right now inventory.js does two jobs: it holds the data and it does the arithmetic. Split it.

  1. Move total() into a new shop/cart.js, which imports items from inventory.js
  2. main.js now imports from three files and does no work of its own
  3. Draw the arrows on paper: which file imports which?

Done when: main.js reads like a summary of the program rather than the program itself. That is the whole reason to split files, and it is worth saying out loud.

Your diagram should have no cycles. If two arrows point at each other, part 5 is about to happen to you.

5 · Break it on purpose — the circular import

Make cart.js import something from inventory.js, and inventory.js import something from cart.js. Run it.

  1. Read the error, or the undefined, carefully — a circular import often does not crash, it just hands you undefined at the wrong moment, which is worse
  2. Fix it by moving the shared thing into a third file that both import
  3. Re-draw your arrows and confirm the cycle is gone

Done when: You have seen what a circular import looks like before it happens to you at 11pm during build season. The fix is always the same shape: pull the shared thing out into its own file.

This is the one genuinely nasty bug in this module. It does not announce itself. Recognising the symptom — a value that is undefined when it obviously should not be — is worth more than any syntax here.

Stretch · Why bundlers exist

Add export const unused = "nobody imports me"; to inventory.js and run again. Nothing changes — Node loads the file regardless.

Now think about a browser. Every import is potentially a separate network request, and unused would be shipped to a user who never touches it.

  1. Read the first three paragraphs of the Vite: Why Vite page
  2. Write two sentences in your log: what problem a bundler solves, and what "tree shaking" removes

Done when: You can say why a browser project needs a build step and a Node script does not. Module 10 is where you meet Vite properly — arriving with this already in your head makes it five minutes instead of an hour.

✅ Check Yourself

Can you, without looking anything up:

  • Write an export and the matching import from memory?
  • Say what "type": "module" does?
  • Explain the difference between a named and a default export?
  • Say why the .js extension is required in Node imports?
  • Describe what a circular import does, and how to fix one?
  • Say what a bundler is for?

If any box is unchecked, spend twenty minutes on that row's resource. Then check it.

🏁 Done When
  • node shop/main.js runs and prints your inventory work
  • You have at least four files that import from each other, and main.js does no arithmetic of its own
  • You caused a circular import, saw what it did, and fixed it
  • Your log entry is written — what you built, what confused you and how you resolved it, any AI use, and the URL of anything you looked up
  • build check: show me your import diagram and talk me through what happened when you made the cycle. Five minutes.

Next: Module 9 — Async JavaScript — promises, async/await, and fetch. That is the module the Data App is actually built on, and it is the one where code stops running top to bottom.

docs.title: Async JavaScriptPart 1 · Module 9 — Async JavaScript
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Module 9

Scheduled Black Tue, Sep 1, 2026 · Gold Wed, Sep 2, 2026

7253 Software Development Capstone · self-guided · work at your own pace

🎯 Objective

By the end of this module you can:

  • Explain why JavaScript does not simply wait
  • Read and write a Promise chain with .then()
  • Rewrite the same thing with async/await
  • fetch real data from a real API
  • Handle a failure — a bad URL, a 404, and no network — without your program dying
🔑 Why it matters

This is the module the P1 Data App is built on. Everything before this was practice; this is the thing your project actually does.

It is also where code stops running top to bottom, which is the single biggest conceptual jump in Part 1. Take the extra day if you need it.

IdeaWhere you meet it again PromisesEvery API call, every file read, every timer async/awaitHow you will write all of it — .then() is mostly for reading other people's code fetchThe Data App. Then useEffect in Part 2, which is this plus React Error handling (D1.7)The difference between an app and a demo. Networks fail; yours has to survive it

Loading and error states are not polish. A page that shows nothing while it waits and a blank screen when it fails is a broken page, and the project rubric asks for both.

📖 Learn TopicGo-to resource Callbacks, then promisesjavascript.info: Introduction to callbacks Promisesjavascript.info: Promise async/awaitjavascript.info: Async/await fetchMDN: Using the Fetch API A free API to practise onPokeAPI · JSONPlaceholder

Read the callbacks page even though you will not write callbacks. It is four minutes and it explains what promises were invented to fix, which makes the rest of the module make sense instead of being syntax you memorise.

The one idea underneath all of it

A promise is a receipt, not the thing.

You ask for data and get a receipt immediately. The data arrives later. await means "stop here until the receipt is honoured" — and everything confusing about async code comes from forgetting that the receipt and the data are not the same object.

⌨️ Build — async.js

In your capstone folder, make async.js. Run it as you go with node async.js. You need internet for parts 4 and 5.

1 · Prove it does not wait 
console.log("first");
setTimeout(() => console.log("second"), 0);
console.log("third");
  1. Predict the order out loud before you run it
  2. Run it
  3. Write one sentence in your log about why second lost to third despite a delay of zero

Done when: You predicted wrong, or you predicted right for the right reason. Zero milliseconds does not mean now — it means "as soon as the current work is finished," and that is the whole model.

If this part feels trivial, you have missed it. Every async bug you will ever write comes from expecting line 2 to finish before line 3.

2 · A promise, by hand 
function wait(ms, value) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(() => resolve(value), ms));
}

wait(500, "done")
  .then((v) => console.log(v))
  .then(() => console.log("and then this"));
  1. Run it and watch the order
  2. Print the promise itself: console.log(wait(500, "x")) — look at what you get immediately
  3. Chain a third .then() that returns a value, and a fourth that prints it

Done when: Item 2 showed you Promise { <pending> }. That is the receipt. The value is not there yet and the program carried on anyway.

Each .then() hands its return value to the next one. That is what makes chains work, and it is why forgetting a return inside a .then() breaks things two links down the chain.

3 · The same thing, readable 
async function run() {
  const v = await wait(500, "done");
  console.log(v);
  console.log("and then this");
}
run();
  1. Write it and confirm it behaves identically to part 2
  2. Remove the await and run it — look at what prints
  3. Put it back. Then try await outside an async function and read the error

Done when: You can convert a .then() chain to async/await and back. Item 2 printed the receipt instead of the value, which is the single most common async mistake there is.

Write async/await; read .then(). You need both because half the examples online are chains, but everything you author from here should use await.

4 · fetch — real data 
async function getPokemon(name) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/pokemon/${name}`);
  const data = await res.json();
  return data;
}

const p = await getPokemon("ditto");
console.log(p.name, p.weight);
  1. Get it printing a name and a weight
  2. Notice there are two awaits and work out what each one is waiting for
  3. Print the whole res object before .json() and find status and ok
  4. Pull out three fields you care about and print them tidily

Done when: You can say what each await is for: the first waits for the response to arrive, the second waits for the body to be parsed. Two separate waits, and skipping the second is why people end up printing a Promise.

Top-level await only works in a module. You set "type": "module" in Module 8 — this is the first place it pays off.

5 · Make it fail — three ways

An app that only works when everything works is a demo. Break it deliberately:

async function getPokemon(name) {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/pokemon/${name}`);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Not found: ${name} (${res.status})`);
    return await res.json();
  } catch (err) {
    console.error("Could not load:", err.message);
    return null;
  }
}
  1. Ask for a pokemon that does not exist and confirm you get your message, not a crash
  2. Break the URL itself (https://pokeapi.invalid/) and see a different kind of failure
  3. Turn your wifi off and run it again
  4. Make the caller handle null without exploding

Done when: All three failures print something a human could act on, and the program keeps running. Note that a 404 does not throw on its own — fetch only rejects when the request itself fails, which is why the res.ok check has to be there.

This is standard D1.7 and the project rubric asks for it. "It worked on my machine with wifi" is not a finished feature.

Stretch · Two at once 
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([
  getPokemon("ditto"),
  getPokemon("pikachu"),
]);
  1. Time two sequential awaits with console.time
  2. Time the Promise.all version
  3. Write down both numbers and the reason for the difference
  4. Now read about Promise.allSettled and say when you would want it instead

Done when: The parallel version takes roughly as long as the slower of the two rather than the sum. You can also say why allSettled exists: Promise.all gives up entirely if any one of them fails.

✅ Check Yourself

Can you, without looking anything up:

  • Explain why setTimeout(fn, 0) does not run immediately?
  • Say what a promise actually is, in one sentence?
  • Convert a .then() chain into async/await?
  • Say what each of the two awaits in a fetch is waiting for?
  • Explain why a 404 does not throw, and what you have to write instead?
  • Say what Promise.all buys you, and what it costs?

If any box is unchecked, spend twenty minutes on that row's resource. Then check it.

🏁 Done When
  • async.js runs and covers all five parts
  • Your fetch survives all three failure modes: bad name, bad host, no network
  • You have the two timing numbers from the stretch
  • Your log entry is written — what you built, what confused you and how you resolved it, any AI use, and the URL of anything you looked up
  • build check: turn your wifi off, run it, and show me it failing gracefully. Five minutes.

Next: Module 10 — Modern Syntax & Tooling — optional chaining, ??, npm, and your first Vite project. Then the P1 Data App, which is this module with a user interface bolted on.

docs.title: P1 Data App — Choose your API & prove the fetch
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Work block

Scheduled Black Wed, Sep 9, 2026 · Gold Thu, Sep 10, 2026

Today's learning target

I can choose an API, read its documentation, and prove I can get data out of it.

One work block. At the end of it, real data from a real API is arriving in your browser.

This is a work block, not a module. There is no new lecture — you are building Project 1, and the requirement numbers below come straight from the project checklist you already have.

What to get done
  1. Choose your API. It must be free, need no server-side key, and return JSON. Pick a subject you actually care about — you are living with it until the end of the semester.
  2. Open the raw URL in a browser tab first. If you cannot see JSON there, nothing you write will help.
  3. Make a project folder with index.html and src/api.js and src/main.js.
  4. Write one async function that fetches the feed and returns response.json().
  5. console.log the result and read the shape. Find where the array of things actually lives — it is rarely at the top.
  6. Dump the JSON onto the page so you can see it without the console open.
Done when
  • You can name your API and what one record represents
  • The raw URL shows JSON in a browser tab
  • Your page shows real data from that API
  • You can point at the array in the response and say where it lives
  • <script type="module"> — without it, import will not work
If you are stuck

Almost every failure today is one of three: the API needs a key it will not give a browser, CORS blocks it, or the array is nested somewhere they have not found. Check the raw URL in a tab before debugging any JavaScript. Requiring a two-tab check up front saves the period.

Before you leave

Commit and push. A work block you cannot get back to is a work block you did not have.

docs.title: P1 Data App — Loading & error states
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Work block

Scheduled Black Tue, Sep 15, 2026 · Gold Wed, Sep 16, 2026

Today's learning target

I can show a loading state, catch a failed request, and tell the user something useful instead of showing a blank page.

What your app does when the network is slow, or gone, or the API has moved.

This is a work block, not a module. There is no new lecture — you are building Project 1, and the requirement numbers below come straight from the project checklist you already have.

What to get done
  1. Add renderLoading(el) and call it before the await, not after. After the await, nobody ever sees it.
  2. Wrap the fetch in try / catch.
  3. Check response.ok and throw yourself. A 404 is a successful request for a page that is not there — fetch does not throw on it, and this surprises everyone exactly once.
  4. Write a function that turns an error into a sentence a person can act on. “Check your connection” is useful; TypeError: Failed to fetch is not.
  5. Add a Try again button in the error state.
  6. Test all three states. Turn your wifi off and reload. Point at a URL that does not exist. Throttle the network in DevTools to see your own loading state.
Done when
  • A loading state appears before the data does
  • Wifi off, reload — a readable message, not a blank page and not a crash
  • A bad URL gives a different message from being offline
  • Try again actually retries
  • You have seen all three states with your own eyes, not just written the code
If you are stuck

The 404 behaviour is the concept of the day: fetch only rejects when the request never happened. A 404 or a 500 resolves normally with ok === false, so an app without that check renders undefined and looks broken for no visible reason. Requirements 2 and 3 on the Project 1 checklist are exactly this.

Before you leave

Commit and push. A work block you cannot get back to is a work block you did not have.

docs.title: P1 Data App — Render real data to the page
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Work block

Scheduled Black Fri, Sep 11, 2026 · Gold Mon, Sep 14, 2026

Today's learning target

I can turn an API response into DOM elements, with the fetching and the drawing in separate modules.

The JSON dump becomes a list a person would want to look at.

This is a work block, not a module. There is no new lecture — you are building Project 1, and the requirement numbers below come straight from the project checklist you already have.

What to get done
  1. Write a function that maps the raw response into the shape your UI wants — just the fields you will show, flat.
  2. Put that in api.js. Put the drawing in a new render.js. Nothing in render.js fetches; nothing in api.js touches the DOM.
  3. Write renderList(el, items) that builds the markup and writes it once.
  4. Style it enough to be readable. This is not the styling block, but a wall of unstyled text hides real problems.
  5. Handle the empty case: what does the page say when the list has zero items?
Done when
  • The page shows a real list, not JSON
  • api.js never touches the DOM; render.js never fetches
  • The mapped objects hold only the fields you actually display
  • An empty list produces a sentence, not a blank page
  • You build the markup once and assign it once, rather than in a loop
If you are stuck

Two things to watch. Building the DOM inside a loop with += on innerHTML re-parses the whole list every pass; have them build a string or an array and assign once. And someone will fetch inside render.js because it is convenient — that is the module boundary collapsing on day one, and it is worth stopping.

Before you leave

Commit and push. A work block you cannot get back to is a work block you did not have.

docs.text:
Godot and Python game programming - the pathway's on-ramp.

The on-ramp to the pathway. Semester 1 builds four games in Godot 4 with GDScript, each one introducing the programming ideas the next one depends on. Semester 2 moves to Python and Pygame with the same project-first approach.

No prior programming experience is assumed. You will write code on day one.

/*
 * U1 L1 — HELLO COMPILER · STARTER CODE
 * 7184 Software Development · Unit 1, Lesson 1
 *
 * This is the first file of your arena game. Every lesson in this unit adds to
 * THIS file — by Lesson 5 it takes input and prints a formatted status line.
 *
 * TO RUN IT — two separate commands, on purpose:
 *
 *     javac Main.java      compiles it. This MAKES Main.class
 *     java Main            runs the .class file. No .java on the end
 *
 * Do them one at a time at least once today. The first command makes the
 * program, the second one runs it. That split is the whole point of Lesson 1,
 * and it is the thing Python never made you think about.
 */
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // Done for you, so you can compile and run before you change anything.
        System.out.println("The arena awaits.");


        // TODO 1: three more lines that open YOUR game.
        //         Not an arena unless you want one — a dungeon, a spaceship,
        //         a haunted kitchen. One System.out.println("..."); per line.
        //         Compile and run after EACH line, not at the end.


        // TODO 2: an empty line in the output. System.out.println("");


        // TODO 3: break it on purpose. Do these ONE AT A TIME, and read the
        //         error out loud before you undo it:
        //
        //           a) delete a semicolon
        //           b) change  System.out.println  to  system.out.println
        //           c) delete one closing quote "
        //
        //         javac gives you a line number and a reason. Three different
        //         mistakes, three different messages. Learning to read them now
        //         is worth more than anything else you do today.

    }
}

src/Main.java
/*
 * U1 L10 — METHODS, PARAMETERS, RETURN VALUES · STARTER CODE
 * 7184 Software Development · Unit 1, Lesson 10
 *
 * ALREADY HERE:  Lessons 1-9 finished. It works. It is also 258 lines long
 *                and every one of them is inside main.
 * YOU'RE ADDING: nothing. Today you MOVE things.
 *
 *     javac Main.java
 *     java Main
 *
 * THE RULE OF THE DAY: BEHAVIOUR MUST NOT CHANGE.
 *
 *   1. Run it now. Play one fight. Write down what happens.
 *   2. Refactor.
 *   3. Run it again. If anything is different, you broke it.
 *
 * That discipline has a name — refactoring — and it is worth more than the
 * syntax you learn today.
 *
 * ==========================================================================
 * YOUR TARGET
 *
 *   main right now:  258 lines
 *   main by the end: under 60
 *
 * Count it before and after. Both numbers go on the board.
 * ==========================================================================
 *
 * HOW TO DO THIS WITHOUT BREAKING IT
 *
 *   Move ONE thing. Compile. Run. Then move the next one.
 *
 *   Moving six methods and then compiling gives you six errors at once and no
 *   idea which change caused which. Moving one gives you one.
 *
 * ==========================================================================
 * THE ORDER TO WORK IN — easiest first, so you get a win early
 *
 * TODO 1: the pure-output ones. No return value; nothing to get subtly wrong.
 *
 *           static void printBanner(String text) {
 *               System.out.println("=".repeat(40));
 *               System.out.printf("  %s%n", text);
 *           }
 *
 *           static void printHealthBar(int hp) { ... }
 *           static void printTitle() { ... }
 *           static void countdown(int from) { ... }
 *
 *         Methods go at CLASS level — as siblings of main, not inside it.
 *         Look at where main's closing brace is and put them after it.
 *
 * TODO 2: the ones that hand a value back.
 *
 *           static boolean isAlive(int hp) {
 *               return hp > 0;
 *           }
 *
 *           static int calculateDamage(int power, int roll) {
 *               if (roll >= 9) return power * 2;
 *               if (roll >= 3) return power;
 *               return 0;
 *           }
 *
 *           static int applyDamage(int hp, int damage) { return hp - damage; }
 *
 *         Three returns in one method is fine. The first one that runs wins.
 *
 * TODO 3: the arena. It is the biggest single block in main and it moves
 *         without changing a character:
 *
 *           static void drawArena(int playerRow, int playerCol,
 *                                 int enemyRow, int enemyCol) { ... }
 *
 *         It needs FOUR parameters because a method cannot see main's local
 *         variables. That is not a limitation to work around — it is the
 *         entire point. The method works for any positions you hand it.
 *
 * TODO 4: the big win — the input validation from Lesson 8.
 *
 *           static int readChoice(Scanner in, int min, int max) {
 *               int choice;
 *               do {
 *                   System.out.printf("Choose %d-%d: ", min, max);
 *                   while (!in.hasNextInt()) {
 *                       in.next();
 *                       System.out.printf("Numbers only. Choose %d-%d: ", min, max);
 *                   }
 *                   choice = in.nextInt();
 *                   in.nextLine();
 *               } while (choice < min || choice > max);
 *               return choice;
 *           }
 *
 *         Twelve lines you fought for in Lesson 8, now one call — and you can
 *         use it anywhere you need a number in a range. THAT is abstraction.
 *
 * TODO 5: OVERLOAD calculateDamage with a crit-multiplier version.
 *
 *           static int calculateDamage(int power, int roll, double critMultiplier)
 *
 *         Same name, different PARAMETER LIST. Two methods that differ only in
 *         return type will not compile — try it once so you see the error.
 *
 * ==========================================================================
 * THE ONE THAT WILL CATCH YOU
 *
 *   static void tryToHeal(int hp) { hp += 50; }   // does NOTHING
 *
 *   Java hands the method a COPY. Changing the copy does not change yours.
 *   The fix is to give it back:
 *
 *       health = heal(health, 50);
 *
 *   When a method "does nothing", this is why. Every time.
 *
 * ==========================================================================
 * FINISHED EARLY?
 *
 *   Extract the entire enemy turn into one method.
 *
 *   You will find you need several values back — the enemy's health, the
 *   damage dealt, whether it is still standing — and there is only one
 *   return. Sit with that for five minutes.
 *
 *   You want to return a whole FIGHTER. In Unit 2 you will.
 *
 * ==========================================================================
 * WHAT TO SUBMIT — THIS IS CHECKPOINT 1
 *
 *   Back up as Arena_CP1_LastnameF and submit it on Canvas.
 *   Your game must behave exactly as it did this morning.
 */

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Your Lesson 9 file goes below, unchanged. Start from YOUR OWN code — the
// point of today is refactoring what you wrote, not typing something new.
//
// If you have lost your L9 work, ask, and start from the L9 solution instead.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

import java.util.Scanner;

public class Main {

    static final int MAX_HEALTH = 100;
    static final int STARTING_GOLD = 20;
    static final int ROWS = 5;
    static final int COLS = 11;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);

        System.out.print("""
                ========================
                     THE ARENA
                ========================
                """);
        System.out.println("Sand, torchlight, and a crowd that has already decided how this ends.");
        System.out.println("The gate opens.");
        System.out.println("");

        System.out.print("What is your name, challenger? ");
        String playerName = in.nextLine().trim();
        if (playerName.isEmpty()) {
            playerName = "Challenger";
        }

        int difficulty;
        do {
            System.out.print("Difficulty (1 = easy, 2 = normal, 3 = brutal): ");
            while (!in.hasNextInt()) {
                System.out.print("Numbers only. Try again: ");
                in.next();
            }
            difficulty = in.nextInt();
        } while (difficulty < 1 || difficulty > 3);
        in.nextLine();

        String difficultyName = switch (difficulty) {
            case 1 -> "Easy";
            case 2 -> "Normal";
            case 3 -> "Brutal";
            default -> "Unknown";
        };
        System.out.println("Difficulty: " + difficultyName);
        System.out.println("");

        int health = MAX_HEALTH;
        int potions = 2;
        int playerRow = 2, playerCol = 1;
        int enemyRow = 2, enemyCol = 9;

        String enemyName = "Cave Goblin";
        int enemyHealth = 30 + difficulty * 15;
        int enemyPower = 4 + difficulty * 3;

        System.out.printf("%-12s HP %3d/%3d  Gold %4d  Lv %d%n",
                          playerName, health, MAX_HEALTH, STARTING_GOLD, 1);
        System.out.println("");

        System.out.printf("%s enters the arena. The %s has %d HP.%n",
                          playerName, enemyName, enemyHealth);
        System.out.print("Press Enter to begin...");
        in.nextLine();
        System.out.println("");

        for (int i = 3; i > 0; i--) {
            System.out.println(i + "...");
        }
        System.out.println("FIGHT!");
        System.out.println("");

        int turnNumber = 1;
        boolean playing = true;
        boolean fled = false;

        while (playing) {
            System.out.println("=".repeat(40));
            System.out.printf("  Turn %d%n", turnNumber);
            System.out.printf("%-12s HP %3d/%3d    %-14s HP %3d%n",
                              playerName, health, MAX_HEALTH, enemyName, enemyHealth);
            System.out.println("");

            for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
                for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
                    if (r == playerRow && c == playerCol)      System.out.print('@');
                    else if (r == enemyRow && c == enemyCol)   System.out.print('X');
                    else if (r == 0 || r == ROWS - 1)          System.out.print('-');
                    else if (c == 0 || c == COLS - 1)          System.out.print('|');
                    else                                       System.out.print(' ');
                }
                System.out.println();
            }
            System.out.println("");

            boolean adjacent = (playerRow == enemyRow) && (Math.abs(playerCol - enemyCol) == 1);
            int roll = (turnNumber * 3) % 10 + 1;
            int damage = 0;

            if (adjacent) {
                System.out.print("[A]ttack  [D]efend  [P]otion  [L]eft  [R]ight  [F]lee: ");
            } else {
                System.out.print("The " + enemyName + " is out of reach.  "
                                 + "[L]eft  [R]ight  [D]efend  [P]otion  [F]lee: ");
            }
            String action = in.nextLine().trim().toUpperCase();

            switch (action) {
                case "A" -> {
                    if (!adjacent) {
                        System.out.println("You swing at empty air. Get closer first.");
                    } else if (roll >= 9) {
                        damage = enemyPower * 2;
                        System.out.println("CRITICAL HIT!");
                    } else if (roll >= 3) {
                        damage = enemyPower;
                        System.out.println("A solid hit.");
                    } else {
                        System.out.println("You miss.");
                    }
                }
                case "L" -> {
                    if (playerCol - 1 < 1) {
                        System.out.println("The wall stops you.");
                    } else {
                        playerCol--;
                        System.out.println("You step left.");
                    }
                }
                case "R" -> {
                    if (playerCol + 1 > COLS - 2) {
                        System.out.println("The wall stops you.");
                    } else if (playerCol + 1 == enemyCol) {
                        System.out.println("The " + enemyName + " blocks your way.");
                    } else {
                        playerCol++;
                        System.out.println("You step right.");
                    }
                }
                case "D" -> {
                    health += 5;
                    System.out.println("You raise your guard and recover 5 HP.");
                }
                case "P" -> {
                    if (potions > 0) {
                        potions--;
                        health += 25;
                        System.out.println("You drink a potion and recover 25 HP.");
                    } else {
                        System.out.println("You reach for a potion. There are none.");
                    }
                }
                case "F" -> {
                    fled = true;
                    System.out.println("You run for the gate. The crowd howls.");
                }
                default -> System.out.println("The crowd jeers. You hesitate and lose the turn.");
            }

            enemyHealth -= damage;

            if (!fled && enemyHealth > 0 && adjacent) {
                health -= enemyPower;
                System.out.printf("The %s strikes back for %d.%n", enemyName, enemyPower);
            }

            if (health > MAX_HEALTH) {
                health = MAX_HEALTH;
            } else if (health < 0) {
                health = 0;
            }

            int bars = health / 5;
            String bar = "#".repeat(bars) + "-".repeat(20 - bars);
            System.out.printf("[%s] %d%%%n", bar, health);

            if (fled) {
                System.out.println("You escape with your life, and nothing else.");
                playing = false;
            } else if (enemyHealth <= 0) {
                System.out.printf("%nThe %s falls! You win on turn %d.%n", enemyName, turnNumber);
                playing = false;
            } else if (health <= 0) {
                System.out.printf("%nYou have fallen on turn %d.%n", turnNumber);
                playing = false;
            }

            turnNumber++;
        }

        System.out.printf("%nThe arena empties after %d turns.%n", turnNumber - 1);
    }
}
